## **FIRST ANNUAL REPORT ON EFFECTS OF PATTERNED BLADES on**

## **Prepared for** :

**Prepared by** : Birds & Bats Unlimited: Environmental Consultants Dr R.E. Simmons / M. Martins

## **1 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY**

The Umoya Energy Wind Farm at Hopefield is the first renewable energy project in the southern hemisphere to trial patterned blades to determine if they reduce avian impacts. This report represents the first 12-months’ monitoring of avian fatalities at the (4) patterned blades painted with two broad Signal Red stripes in relation to (16) un-patterned control turbines close by. From nine turbines with high fatality rates, four turbines (T28, T31, T34, T35) were chosen for blade-patterning, each with a nearest neighbour control.

The Umoya carcass searching team completed 12-months of post-treatment surveys from April 2023 to April 2024 and recorded, mainly, Bokmakierie and Cape Spurfowl, but also pigeons, korhaans, Black shouldered Kites and a Peregrine Falcon as bird-strike victims. Their results were compared with two pre-treatment years of monitoring using identical methods to determine pre-patterning fatality rates.

With tower impacts (of Cape Spurfowl and Dikkop) removed, the 12 months’ of post-treatment monitoring revealed a total of 10 fatalities at the total 20 turbines:  0 at the (4) patterned blades and 10 at the (16) controls. The expected number of fatalities after the painting, based on the fatality rates before painting revealed that the four patterned turbines had fewer fatalities (0) than expected (6.5) – indicating a 100% reduction in fatalities for all bird species. This cannot be explained as an overall decrease in fatalities since the un-patterned control turbines had similar numbers of fatalities in the same experimental period (10) as expected (12.0).

Statistical tests comparing observed vs expected fatalities – before and after treatment – for the patterned vs all (16) un-patterned controls were Significant at the p = 0.027 level. Higher significance (p = 0.007) was found when the patterned turbines were comparted with the (4) nearest neighbours. No raptors were killed at the patterned blades after treatment, despite six species accounting for seven fatalities prior to treatment.

These results were not affected by omitting species (e.g. spurfowl) believed to be killed by flying into the towers. The inclusion of all (20) Spurfowl and a Dikkop carcass found as fatalities at the tower bases did not change the significance of patterned blades vs all (16) controls (p = 0.038), or the patterned vs nearest neighbours (p<0.009).

Thus, results at the Umoya Wind Farm indicate that patterning the blades significantly reduces the number of avian fatalities. That it did so after just 12 months, and by 100% for all species, was unexpectedly efficient. While these are small samples, they exceed those achieved with a solid black design in Norway (May et al. 2020: 72%) and are more significant than the unpublished Dutch study (Klop et al. 2024), also with a solid black design.

Further fatality data through 2024 and 2025 will increase the sample sizes and confidence of these first Umoya results and allow a robust assessment over two years. The positive outcome of this study should give confidence to the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) to permit other wind facilities in South Africa,  to implement and test this mitigation in areas of high avian diversity.

Based on comparison with other experiments BBU recommends that patterned rather than solid designs may give the best results for reducing avian fatalities.

## **2 INTRODUCTION**

Renewable energy in the form of wind and solar farms provides sustainable green energy with minimal greenhouse gases in a rapidly warming world. Despite these considerable benefits there are environmental costs in terms of species of birds and bats killed by spinning blades and grid connections.

In South Africa, turbines kill on average 4.4 + 2.9 birds per year, or 2.0 + 1.3 birds per MW per year (Perold et al. 2020). And unlike other countries a high diversity of species are killed covering 130 species from 46 families ranging from the smallest waxbills to the largest Martial Eagles (Perold et al. 2020, Simmons and Martins 2024). This review also revealed that the most vulnerable group were raptors (hawks, harriers, eagles, owls) comprising over a third (36%) of the 848 carcasses recovered (Perold et al. 2020).  This is in line with other reports of a high toll of raptors elsewhere in South Africa and globally (Simmons and Martins 2019, Thaxter et al. 2017).

Many methods of mitigation have been mooted to reduce this environmental cost – among these is patterning the blades to increase their visibility to passing raptors (May et al. 2020). This is potentially the least financially costly relative to other automated shut down on demand (SDOD) methods.

The Umoya Wind Farm (UWF) in Hopefield is the first to trial this form of mitigation in Africa at the recommendation of Birds & Bats Unlimited (BBU). Umoya successfully convinced the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) to allow patterned blades, but CAA dis-allowed black paint to be used (as in the Norway experiment). Instead, they permitted “Signal Red” as their legislation already allowed this on tall communication towers.

Thus, one blade of four turbines was painted with two broad red stripes as recommended by McIsaac (2001), in early 2023. BBU recommended that turbines with the highest fatality records were treated and that their nearest neighbours and 12 others be used as two sets of controls.

The outcome of this first experiment for the African continent is important not only for the UWF but for other developers in South Africa, as it allows insights into the efficacy of such mitigations. Permitting from CAA has now become easier given that in November 2023 the South African Wind Energy Association (SAWEA) successfully motivated (Morkel et al. 2023) to the CAA for a blanket permit allowing all wind farms the opportunity for patterning their blades.

This “Alternative Means of Compliance” (AMOC) was granted by the SA CAA on 18 January 2024 SAWEA Exemption Outcome letter V1.pdf  allowing the South African wind industry the opportunity to pattern their blades. The Umoya example is leading the way in the first field test in Africa and the southern hemisphere.

This first annual report assesses the first 12 months’ of carcass monitoring from April 2023 to April 2024 for the operational Umoya Wind Farm in Hopefield.

Here we compare:

- the fatalities for the (4) **patterned turbines** before and after patterning with Signal Red, with

- the fatalities for the (16) **un-patterned (Control) turbines** in the same before-after periods.

- We also compared fatalities with the (4) **nearest neighbour (Control)** turbines.

- Avian fatalities from 12 months in 2014-2015 (Arcus Consulting 2016) and 12 months in 20202021 (BBU 2021) were used as the controls before any patterning took place.

Our aims here are to understand the effects of patterning the four Umoya turbines in terms of:

- (i) any reduction in fatalities at the (4) patterned vs their (4) un-patterned nearest neighbours,

- (ii) fatalities at the (4) patterned blades vs (16) un-patterned blades before and after treatment, and

- (iii) determining if patterning at some turbines increases the collision rate at the neighbouring (unpatterned) turbines.

Our _a-priori_ prediction is that the number of fatalities will decrease at the patterned turbines (but not the controls) because all birds – and particularly raptors – are more likely to see and avoid the higher contrast blades.

- 2.1 Background to the Umoya Wind Farm

- The Umoya Wind Farm comprises 37 Vestas 1.8 MW wind turbines with a capacity of 66.6 MW.

- It is situated 5-km south-east of Hopefield, straddling the R45 in the Saldanha Bay Municipality, Western Cape.

- Umoya Energy owns three adjoining farms with a combined area of approximately 2400 hectares. Roughly half of this land was designated as a Conservation Area managed by SANParks and will be declared part of the West Coast National Park.

- Umoya Energy Wind Farm received Environmental Authorisation in September 2009.

- Construction of the wind farm commenced in December 2012.

- Commercial production of energy for the South African grid commenced in February 2014.

Because it was felt that threatened Red Data species may be at risk on this farm the Department of Environment (now Department of Forestry, Fisheries and Environment, DFFE) requested that further avian monitoring be undertaken to check this possibility.  This has been achieved (Arcus 2016, BBU 2021) and the present carcass searching has been underway since April 2023.

The patterning of the blades took place _in situ_ from January to March 2023 and carcass searching began in mid-April 2023, covering 20 turbines, inclusive of the four patterned blades, weekly to twice monthly.

## **3 METHODS**

The carcass survey methods employed by Arcus in 2014-2015 at the Umoya Wind Facility (UWF) were repeated for the Hopefield carcass search teams in 2020/2021. They used four Environment Survey Assistants (ESAs), working in two pairs at different turbines, and searched for bird and bat carcasses at all 37 turbines at the WEF site from 15 December 2014 to 15 December 2015. This was repeated for 20 turbines in the present 12-months of monitoring. The turbines surveyed were reduced to allow carcass searchers to concentrate their efforts on the (4) patterned turbines and their  (16) immediate neighbours. Arcus created search plots with an 80-m radius from each turbine base, in which the ESAs searched for bird and bat carcasses. Circular transects were walked slowly by each pair of ESAs, who remained approximately six metres apart.

**The search interval** (i.e., the number of days between searches at individual turbines) was seven days. A search schedule for the entire year was created such that the turbines were searched weekly and each turbine covered an equal number of times per year. In total, the number of searches per turbine ranged from 46 to 55, totalling 1866 searches, with differences resulting from logistical reasons, for example holidays, torrential rain, or turbine maintenance.  On two occasions when a control turbine (T26) was offline, an adjacent turbine (T27) was employed as the control for the duration (70 days: June - August 2023 and 15 days: November - December 2023). On one occasion the patterned turbine T28 was offline for a week (16-23 August), but no similarly treated turbine could be used in its place.

Each observer was instructed to look for any evidence of possible bird or bat fatalities (regardless of the possible cause of the fatality). They were also instructed to complete fatality reports for any carcasses found outside of the regular search schedule – for example by the onsite staff (including maintenance and security staff) – or while the ESAs travelled around the WEF. All evidence was collected and stored onsite in a freezer and examined by the Bird Specialist to determine the species involved and the most likely cause of death. In the current 12-months monitoring period (April 2023 to April 2024) all carcasses were photographed _in situ_ with a photograph of the GPS coordinates and the closest turbine. These were identified as far as possible by RE Simmons, and extra information was sometimes requested.

Given that biases in the form of carcass removal by scavengers and observers over-looking carcasses can occur, Arcus also set up trials to determine the biases from both sources. This was not repeated in 2020-2021 or in the year under review since site visits were not part of the Terms of Reference.

Large numbers of Cape Spurfowl were found in these pre-treatment surveys, and Arcus (2016) suspected that these birds were hitting the towers and not being killed by the blades. The ESAs in this (2023/24) phase also suspected tower collisions, as many of these birds were found within a few metres of the towers.

Given that the experiments are focused on the ability of birds to avoid high visibility blades and not the towers, all the Spurfowls, and one Dikkop also found next to the tower (with an impact mark on the tower) were removed from the analysis. This removed 12 (of 50) individual birds from the “Before” group, and 8 (of 18) from the “After” group. This reduced the sample size and, thus, the power of the tests but was felt to be more biologically accurate.

Similar observations for fast-flying, low-agility game birds were made in Norway where Willow Ptarmigan _Lagopus lagopus_ collide with towers (Stokke et al. 2020), and this has also been reported in Spain (F Cervantes pers comm). The tower-strikes were also removed from their analyses.

## 3.1 Study area and experimental design

The UWF turbines chosen for patterning were from those exhibiting either:

(i) the highest overall fatalities based on the previous sampling; or

(ii) fatalities to Red Data species.

Of the nine turbines that fell within these parameters, four were chosen for treatment: T28, T31, T34, T35 (see Table 1 for details). The locations of these are shown in Figure 1. For each treated turbine its nearest neighbour was chosen as a (unpainted) control turbine. An additional 12 un-patterned turbines were also used as controls for other analyses. All of these turbines fell in a “high impact” zone in the northern section of the UWF.

The study area lies within the Fynbos biome, in _Endangered_ Hopefield Sand Fynbos (Mucina and Rutherford 2011). Vegetation is intact but previously farmed throughout the farm. It lies in a winter rainfall area with a mean annual precipitation of 326-mm and mean maximum temperature of 28.3[o] C and minimum of 7.1[o] C. Misty days are common in winter (Mucina and Rutherford 2011). Daylight hours for Cape Town  range from 14.25 hours at the height of summer to 9.54 hours in winter (Sunrise and sunset in Cape Town (timeanddate.no)

## 3.2 Statistical tests

Note that the Chi-square ( _X_[2] ) test statistic used here to test for significant differences is given for indicative purposes only because it does not handle small numbers (such as zeros) very well. Each test was repeated with the Barnard’s Unconditional Test that is more appropriate for small samples. The results were identical to the _X_[2] tests, so we have retained the _X_[2 ] test results here. Once future fatalities are sampled under the patterned and control turbines then more sophisticated statistical tests (Generalized Linear Models [GLMs]) will be undertaken by Dr F Cervantes. Initial tests, done to date largely support the less sophisticated tests here.

**Figure 1:** The location of the four patterned blades (= large red triangles) relative to the other (16) un-patterned turbines (= blue triangles) within the study areas (= red polygon) in the Umoya Wind Farm at Hopefield. The study area was reduced from the full 37 turbines to 20 to make the sampling more comprehensive and focussed.

## **4 RESULTS**

## 4.1 Historical avian fatalities occurring on the Umoya Wind farm 2014-15 and 2020-21.

Two years of bird fatality surveys were undertaken across the wind farm in 2014-2015 and 2020-2021 (Table 1). A total of 75 bird strikes of 23 species were recorded at the 37 turbines over 24 months, ascribed to collision with the turbines. That gives a low fatality rate (unadjusted) of 1.01 birds/turbine/yr. Employing the adjustment rate of 1.92 (Arcus 2016) to account for observer bias and scavenger removal, the fatality rate becomes 1.93 birds/turbine/yr. Still a very low rate.

The identification of “problem” turbines was used to choose where the patterned blade mitigation would best be focussed for conservation purposes. Overall, they were responsible for 50% of the 75 known avian fatalities over 24 months. The four turbines chosen for patterning were responsible for 25% of all 75 fatalities (n=19), with spurfowl included. These turbines were T28, T31, T34, and T35 and were each responsible for three or more fatalities. This included a total of seven raptor fatalities and notably an _Endangered_ Black Harrier, prior to treatment. With spurfowl removed, fatalities for most turbines was reduced to three birds, with a maximum of four fatalities at T35. The nine turbines were then responsible for 47% of 55 deaths.

Because avian fatality rates were recorded before and after patterning, we can use the powerful BACI test (where B =  Before, A = After, C = Control, I = Impact) to statistically test the effect of experimentally patterning the “Impact” turbines on fatalities before and after treatment. These are given in the legends of each figure.

## 4.2 Avian fatalities at the Patterned turbines vs all Control turbines

During the present 12 months monitoring a total of 18 avian fatalities were recorded: 16 at the unpatterned turbines, and two at the patterned turbines (Table 3, Appendix 1). Eight of the 18 were spurfowl or dikkops, presumed to be tower deaths, and were removed from further analysis. Thus, 10 fatalities were recorded, all at the control turbines and none at the patterned turbines. We can interpret this result by calculating the number of fatalities that were expected.

Given that the _previous rates_ of fatality were:

   - 24 birds in 24 months at the 16 control turbines (= 0.063 fatalities/turbine/month) and

   - 13 birds in 24 months at the 4 turbines to be patterned (= 0.135 fatalities/turbine/month) then,

- over 12 months we **expect** :

   - at the 16 control turbines (16*12*0.063 =) **12.0 fatalities** and

   - at the **4 patterned turbines** (4*12*0.135 =) **6.5 fatalities.**

However, as shown in Table 3, the number of fatalities recorded at the patterned blades in 12 months was 0 (zero) birds, not 6.5 birds. The number of fatalities recorded at the (16) control turbines, however, was similar to that expected (10 vs 12.0).

## **Thus, it appears that the number of deaths occurring at the patterned blades showed a 100% reduction – (0 vs 6.5), and this was not due to a general decrease in overall fatalities.**

Note too that raptors were not absent from the Umoya Wind Farm (which might explain the low fatality rates). This was borne out by the loss of two Black shouldered Kites and a Peregrine Falcon at the 16 Control turbines in the 12 months under review (Appendix 1). Other species killed were Cape Spurfowls (removed from the analysis), Southern Black Korhaan, Bokmakierie, canaries, pigeons and a Little Grebe.

Observations of live birds at the farm in September/October 2023 by RES and bird specialist Eric Herrmann also recorded five raptor species present and active on the farm including: Jackal Buzzard (x2) breeding, Yellow-billed Kite (x4), Black-shouldered Kite (x3) breeding, Rock Kestrel x2 and Black Harrier (x1).

All were recorded around the north-western section of the farm, where the patterned blades are being trialled and this suggests these species were avoiding turbines that had previously proven fatal.

Prior to painting, 13 fatalities were recorded over two years at the turbines chosen for patterning. After they were patterned no further fatalities were recorded in 12 months. The controls showed a different pattern (6 fatalities before any patterning and 5 fatalities since patterning of the neighbours). This indicates that the lack of fatalities at the patterned blades was not due to a decrease in overall bird numbers, but likely due to the patterning itself. The results were highly significant (P = 0.007, Figure 3).

Thus, the nearest neighbour comparisons indicate with higher probability that the patterned blades significantly reduced the number of fatalities relative to their nearest neighbours in 12 months.

## 4.4 Do birds seeing the patterned blades divert into the nearest neighbours?

A potentially confounding issue of patterning blades is that once birds see them, they could veer away and into nearby turbines, increasing the fatality rate at the nearest neighbours. This possibility was checked by comparing fatality rates of the nearest neighbours (NN) before and after patterning, with the other (12) controls before and after patterning. There was no significant effect (Figure 4). In other words, there was no increase in the number of fatalities at the nearest neighbours of the experimental turbines, relative to the other controls. This potential side effect does not appear to be an issue at the Umoya Wind Farm, and it was, likewise, not an effect at the Smøla wind farm in Norway (May et al. 2020).

**Figure 4** :  Avian fatalities of nearest neighbours (nn) before and after painting (left hand bars) relative to the other (12) controls before and after painting of the four experimental turbines (not shown). There was no significant increase in fatalities at the nearest neighbours after the treatment ( _X_[2] = 1.15, df = 1, _p_ > 0.1) suggesting that birds are not veering into neighbouring turbines when avoiding painted ones.

## 4.5 The role of towers in avian deaths

This analysis of fatalities at the Umoya Wind Farm focussed on birds being killed by the turbine blades. However, some birds appear to be killed by impacting the towers, especially Cape Spurfowl.  This was first recognised by the Arcus carcass search teams (Arcus 2016) and has been suspected by the Umoya ESAs in the season under review. Many spurfowl carcasses are found within a few metres of the tower and their heavy wing loading in combination with their dawn and dusk flights, in small flocks, suggest they don’t see the white towers and impact them. One Spotted Dikkop, a known nocturnal species, was also found less than 2-m from a tower and an impact mark about 8-m high was found on the tower (N Mackay pers comm). All of these birds were removed from analysis reported here, as the experiment was designed to test increased visibility of the blades, not the towers.

The question becomes: what is the effect on the statistical power if they are not removed? That is, if all the birds presumed to be killed by the towers are retained in the analyses. We re-analysed all comparisons with all spurfowl and dikkops included (n = 20 birds) and found that the effect of patterned turbines on fatalities had no influence on the results (Table 5).

**Table 5** . A comparison of the _X_[2] tests for Significance for avian fatalities at patterned and un-patterned turbines with all presumed tower victims included and excluded.

|Comparison|Tower victims**included**|Tower victims**excluded**|
|Patterned Blades vs Nearest neighbours|_X_2= 6.84, P = 0.009|_X_2= 7.46   P = 0.007|
|Patterned blades vs All Controls|_X_2=4.28, P = 0.038|_X_2= 4.86   P = 0.027|
|All Controls vs Nearest Neighbours|_X_2= 2.13, not significant|_X_2= 1.15 not significant|
|Reduction in fatalities at Patterned turbines|80%|100%|

The inclusion of presumed tower victims made no difference in comparisons of the (4) nearest neighbour with the patterned blades, nor was the Significance affected for the comparisons with all (16) controls and patterned blades. Comparing controls with controls (to answer the question do birds veer away from the patterned blades into the nearest neighbours) we also find no effect including or excluding spurfowl (Table 5). The only change was a reduction in fatalities at the patterned blades where two tower victims (a Cape Spurfowl and a Spotted Dikkop) decreased the effect from a 100% drop in fatalities to 80%. For raptors, the decrease in fatalities remained at 100% (7 victims to 0 victims). Thus, the results are robust with or without the inclusion of presumed tower fatalities.

**In summary** , the patterning of four turbine blades resulted in significant reductions in fatalities whether they are compared with all other unpainted (control) turbines or compared with just their four nearest neighbouring controls. Given that 6.5 fatalities were expected (based on pre-treatment fatality rates) at the patterned blades in the 12 months’ following patterning, and none were recorded, the patterning of blades appears to make blades more visible to all birds.

Furthermore, there were no more raptors killed, post-treatment, despite seven individuals of six raptors species being killed by the blades pre-treatment. Thus, the patterning also seems to be effective for the most highly collision-prone species – raptors. These samples are small and represent only 12 months of monitoring by the Umoya team, but they are, nevertheless, hugely promising results. A further 12 months’  will increase confidence in understanding their long-term efficacy.

## **5 COSTS AND COMMERCIAL CONSIDERATIONS**

## 5.1 Cost of Works

The works required the provision of a specialist platform, suspended from the nacelle of the wind turbine, to provide safe access for the technicians to carry out the works. The total cost of the provision of specialist equipment, crane hire, specialist labour, materials and general consumables amounted to a total cost of R 2.46m for the 4 turbines.

## 5.2 Impact on electricity production

Every effort was taken to conduct the required works during periods of low wind, thereby minimising the impact on electricity production, but this has to be considered against the costs of having hired

equipment (most specifically the platform) standing idle while incurring ongoing hire costs. In total the time required to take each of the 4 turbines out of service to complete the works resulted in a total loss of generation revenue of R 328 000.

## 5.3 Warranty and commercial considerations

In this specific instance Vestas, the Original Equipment Supplier and Operator of the wind turbines, agreed to maintain the exact same warranty terms for the patterned turbines. That said, the risk of major component failure lies with the project owners. The weight of the two coats of paint applied to each blade totalled 26.4 kg and both Vestas and the Management team will continue to monitor the performance of the painted turbines to establish whether or not there is any noticeable impact on the wear of critical components of these turbines as a result of this additional weight being applied to a single blade.

## 5.4 Future cost considerations

Umoya note that the cost of retrospectively painting wind turbine blades is significant (in the case of Umoya R607 000 per turbine), especially for wind farms with a large number of wind turbines. However, where patterned blades are ordered as part of the supply of new wind turbines to new projects, the cost of such work in-factory is negligible, if any.

## **6 CONCLUSIONS**

The operational Umoya Wind Farm at Hopefield is the first such farm in the southern hemisphere, or Africa, to experiment with patterning their turbine blades to reduce avian impacts. Single blades at four turbines were painted with two broad Signal Red stripes (as recommended by McIsaac 2001) early in 2023 to determine the subsequent effect on avian fatality rates at these turbines. The Umoya carcass searching team completed the first 12-months of carcass surveys from April 2023 to April 2024.

Their results were compared with two previous years’ monitoring using identical methods and found:

- Most of the present-day fatalities were Bokmakieries and Cape Spurfowl, but included two raptor species – Peregrine Falcon and Black shouldered Kites, as well as korhaans, grebes, doves, and canary;

- The spurfowl were removed from further analysis because they may be chiefly tower collision victims;

- The four turbines given a patterned blade were T28, T31, T34, T35 as these turbines previously showing high fatality rates (with spurfowl). These were compared with 16 un-patterned controls as well as their four nearest neighbours.

- In  the 12-months since the experiment began, no fatalities were recorded at the four patterned turbines. Elsewhere, 10 fatalities were recorded at the white control turbines.

- Did patterning lead to fewer fatalities? The expected number of fatalities at the patterned turbines after treatment, based on their fatality rates before treatment (13 in 24 months) indicate that they had fewer fatalities after 12 months (0 birds) than expected (6.5 birds).

- This was not due to a general decrease in fatalities because the un-patterned turbines had similar numbers of fatalities (10) as that expected (12.0).

- A simple _X_[2] statistical test of the observed vs expected fatalities for (4) patterned vs all (16) control turbines indicates a significant difference before and after (p = 0.027).

- A second _X_[2 ] test of the observed vs expected fatalities for the patterned turbines vs their (4) nearest neighbours showed an even more significant result (p < 0.007). That is, the result is unlikely to be due by chance alone.

- To check if removing tower-victims made any difference to the results, we added all 20 victims back to the analysis and found no difference in the significance values for all comparisons.

- All statistical tests were repeated with Barnard’s Unconditional test and found to give identical probabilities as the _X_[2] tests.

- The costs of retrospectively painting blades on the Umoya wind farm was significant, but the cost of doing so on new projects is likely to be minimal, if any.

## **We conclude that the initial results of the first 12 months’ of monitoring of the four patterned and 16**

## **surrounding white turbines are very promising as they show a 100% reduction in (unadjusted) fatalities for the patterned blades, relative to that expected from previous fatalities at the same turbines.**

That this occurred over a period of just 12 months was unexpectedly efficient and suggests other wind farms would benefit from this simple mitigation measure. The samples are still low given the low fatality rate at the Umoya farm and, thus, the experiment should continue for a further 12 months.

## 6.1 Comparisons with other studies

It is worth noting that the results obtained from this Africa-first experiment have achieved higher reductions in avian fatalities (100%) than the only other published experiment with a black blade mitigation in Norway where a 71.9% reduction in fatalities was achieved for all bird species (May et al. 2020).  It also gives significant results that were not achieved in the Dutch black-blade experiments (with seven turbines and their neighbouring controls) on the coast at Eemshaven after 12 months (Klop et al. 2024).

The Norwegian study however, found a remarkable (100%) reduction in eagle deaths at the four blackpainted turbines after 10 years, with the unpainted turbines continuing to kill eagles at a rate of six per year (Stokke et al. 2024). We achieved similar results but with much smaller samples: seven raptors of six species were killed at the four patterned turbines prior to painting at Umoya (Black Harrier, Booted Eagle, Buzzard spp, Rock Kestrel, Jackal Buzzard x2, Barn Owl) but since patterning no raptors have been killed in 12 months.

Thus, both experiments indicate that the most frequently killed suite of birds –raptors – avoid turbine blades made more visible with black or red paint.

A Spanish study underway at Navarre with black blades, run by Iberdrola, has yet to publish its findings, which may suggest it, too, is not achieving similarly clear-cut results. We suggest that the rapid success achieved at Umoya could be due to the use of a patterning design (two broad stripes) rather than a solid black design. It is unlikely to arise from the use of red rather than black paint as the high contrast achieved by black and white is known to be the best colour combination visible to raptors (Potier et al 2018, Martin and Banks 2023).

As such, we suggest that patterns (two stripes) rather than a solid design in signal red or black may be the best option to increase visibility. We must await further results from these and other field experiments before any firm conclusions can be reached.
